claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations and well-characterized interfacial microstructures.
High-resolution in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction and digital image correlation can capture pre-yield lattice-strain shifts and diffraction-peak changes during quasi-static tensile testing.
The proposed measurements can capture post-yield microstructural evolution, including indicators of crack nucleation.
The in situ data will be used as inputs for an ML surrogate predicting global mechanical properties.
Testing is proposed at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading at approximately 1×10^-4 s^-1.
Hierarchical chemical fluctuations and multiscale interfaces mediate load transfer and yield initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical chemical fluctuations and multiscale interfaces mediate microcrack propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Diffraction-peak parameters and local strain fields directly represent the microstructural mediators connecting evolution of the heterostructure to macroscopic mechanical behavior.
Pre-yield lattice-strain shifts and diffraction-peak broadening or splitting are statistically correlated with Young's modulus and yield strength.
Post-yield crack-nucleation indicators are statistically correlated with toughness.
An ML surrogate can learn the mapping from these in situ markers to Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Learning this marker-to-property mapping can bypass extensive computational simulations and enable rapid prediction.
The methodology will reduce prediction errors by approximately 40% relative to existing simulation-based methods.
Prediction uncertainties will be below 15% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The methodology will improve throughput by a factor of 5–10 relative to existing simulation-based methods.
Reliability may diminish outside room temperature or at higher strain rates.
Reliability may diminish for materials lacking the specific hierarchical heterostructure of HfNbTiVAl10.
Failure to capture post-yield markers associated with crack nucleation will compromise predictability.
Unmeasured factors may contribute to toughness variation beyond what the selected in situ markers capture.

The proposed hypothesis is falsified if any blinded property prediction exceeds 15% uncertainty or if crack-initiation and post-yield predictions show systematic discrepancies from direct measurements.
